q-8.2-manage-quality.title: 8.2 Manage Quality: quality assurance, data representation tools, audits, Design for X, problem solving, improvement methods
q-8.2-manage-quality.notes: Translate the quality management plan into executable quality activities incorporating organisational quality policies; key benefits: higher probability of meeting quality objectives; identify ineffective processes and causes of poor quality; uses Control Quality data to report overall quality status; performed throughout. Sometimes called quality assurance, but broader: in projects QA focuses on the processes used - using them effectively and following standards to assure stakeholders the product will meet needs; Manage Quality includes all QA activities plus product design aspects and process improvements; it falls under conformance work in COQ. Purposes: design an optimal, mature product via design guidelines; build confidence that future output will meet requirements (quality audits, failure analysis); confirm quality processes are used and meet objectives; improve process efficiency and effectiveness. The organisation's QA department may do failure analysis, design of experiments and quality improvement. Manage Quality is everybody's work - PM, team, sponsor, performing organisation management, even the customer; in agile all team members do it throughout; in traditional projects specific members are often responsible. Inputs: quality management plan (acceptable quality level, how to ensure it, handling nonconforming products and corrective action); documents (lessons learned, quality control measurements - evaluate processes and deliverables against standards and validate measurement correctness, quality metrics - basis for test scenarios and improvement, risk report - sources of overall risk affecting quality objectives); OPAs (quality management system, templates incl. check sheets, traceability matrices, test plans, previous audit results, lessons learned). Tools: data gathering - checklists (structured, usually component-specific tool to verify steps were performed or requirements satisfied; should include scope baseline acceptance criteria); data analysis - alternatives analysis, document analysis (quality, test, performance reports and variance analyses point to processes out of control), process analysis (improvement opportunities, problems, constraints, non-value-added activities), root cause analysis (underlying reason for a variance, defect or risk; one root cause may drive several; removing all root causes stops recurrence); decision making - multicriteria decision analysis (implementation scenarios, suppliers; product decisions on life-cycle cost, schedule, satisfaction, defect-resolution risk); data representation - affinity diagrams (group potential causes of defects), cause-and-effect diagrams (fishbone, why-why, Ishikawa: break the problem statement into branches to find root cause; Figure 8-9 example 'product quality not matching requirements' with branches management, environment, material, equipment, process, people), flowcharts (steps leading to a defect), histograms (numerical data: defects per deliverable, ranking of causes, noncompliance counts), matrix diagrams, scatter diagrams (relationship between two variables, e.g., a process element and a defect); audits (structured, independent process to determine compliance with organisational and project policies, processes and procedures; usually by a team external to the project - internal audit, PMO or external auditor; objectives: identify good/best practices, nonconformity, gaps and shortcomings; share good practices; proactively help improve processes and productivity; add to the lessons learned repository; correcting deficiencies should reduce COQ and raise acceptance; scheduled or random, internal or external; can confirm implementation of approved changes); Design for X (DfX: technical guidelines applied during design to optimise a specific aspect - reliability, deployment, assembly, manufacturing, cost, service, usability, safety, quality; may cut cost, improve quality and performance, customer satisfaction); problem solving (define the problem, identify root cause, generate solutions, choose the best, implement, verify effectiveness - from Control Quality findings or audits); quality improvement methods (from QC findings, audits or problem solving; PDCA and Six Sigma most common). Outputs: quality reports (graphical, numerical or qualitative; escalated quality issues, improvement recommendations, corrective action recommendations - rework, defect/bug repair, 100% inspection - and summary of Control Quality findings); test and evaluation documents (from industry needs and templates; inputs to Control Quality; may include checklists and detailed RTMs); change requests; plan updates (quality management plan, scope, schedule, cost baselines); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, risk register). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

q-8.3-control-quality.title: 8.3 Control Quality: check sheets, statistical sampling, inspection, testing, control charts, verified deliverables
q-8.3-control-quality.notes: Monitor and record results of quality activities to assess performance and ensure outputs are complete, correct and meet customer expectations; key benefit: verifying deliverables and work meet key stakeholders' requirements for final acceptance; determines whether outputs do what they were intended to do and comply with standards, requirements, regulations and specifications; performed throughout. Measures completeness, compliance and fitness for use before user acceptance and final delivery, demonstrating with reliable data that acceptance criteria are met. Effort varies by industry (stricter in pharmaceutical, health, transportation, nuclear); in agile all members perform it throughout; in waterfall at specific times toward the end of a project or phase by specified members. Inputs: quality management plan; documents (lessons learned, quality metrics, test and evaluation documents); approved change requests (defect repairs, revised work methods, revised schedules - implementation must be verified, confirmed complete, retested and certified; partial completion causes inconsistencies and delays); deliverables (from 4.3, inspected against acceptance criteria in the scope statement); work performance data (observations, quality metrics, technical performance measures, schedule and cost performance); EEFs (PMIS and quality management software, agency regulations, application-area standards); OPAs (quality standards and policies, templates such as check sheets and checklists, issue and defect reporting procedures). Tools: data gathering - checklists; check sheets (tally sheets organising facts to collect data on a potential quality problem; useful for attribute data during inspections, e.g., frequency of defect types - Figure 8-12: small scratch, large scratch, bent, missing component, wrong colour, labelling error by date); statistical sampling (inspect part of a population, e.g., 10 of 75 drawings at random; frequency and size set in Plan Quality Management); questionnaires and surveys (customer satisfaction after deployment; defects found this way count as external failure costs); data analysis - performance reviews (quality metrics vs actual results), root cause analysis (source of defects); inspection (examination of a work product for conformance to documented standards; any level from a single activity to the final product; also called reviews, peer reviews, audits, walkthroughs; also verifies defect repairs); testing/product evaluations (organised investigation giving objective information about quality per requirements; aims to find errors, defects, bugs; type and extent set in the quality plan; throughout and at the end - early testing lowers the cost of fixing; software: unit, integration, black-box, white-box, interface, regression, alpha; construction: cement strength, concrete workability, nondestructive tests, soil tests; hardware: environmental stress screening, burn-in, system testing); data representation - cause-and-effect diagrams, control charts (whether a process is stable/predictable; upper and lower specification limits come from requirements - maximum and minimum allowed; upper and lower control limits are different, calculated statistically to show the natural capability of a stable process; used to decide where corrective action is taken; used for manufactured lots but also cost and schedule variances, volume, frequency of scope changes), histograms (defects by source or component), scatter diagrams (planned vs actual performance); meetings - approved change requests review (verify implemented as approved, partial changes completed, tested, certified) and retrospectives/lessons learned (what succeeded, what to improve, what to carry into this and future projects, what to add to OPAs). Outputs: quality control measurements (documented results in the format set in the quality plan); verified deliverables (correctness determined; input to Validate Scope for formal acceptance; changed deliverables are re-inspected and re-verified); work performance information (requirements fulfilment, causes of rejection, rework needed, corrective action recommendations, verified deliverables list, quality metric status, need for process adjustments); change requests; plan updates (quality management plan); document updates (issue log - a nonconforming deliverable is often logged as an issue, lessons learned, risk register, test and evaluation documents). Data flow: deliverables and WPD from 4.3; approved change requests from 4.6; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6; verified deliverables to 5.5.

r-resource-overview.title: Project Resource Management overview: six processes, team vs physical resources, trends (EI, self-organising, virtual teams), tailoring, agile
r-resource-overview.section: 9 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 9-1)
r-resource-overview.notes: Identify, acquire and manage resources needed for success; right resources at the right time and place. Processes: 9.1 Plan Resource Management (how to estimate, acquire, manage and utilise physical and team resources); 9.2 Estimate Activity Resources (team resources and type and quantities of material, equipment, supplies); 9.3 Acquire Resources (obtain team members, facilities, equipment, materials, supplies); 9.4 Develop Team (improve competencies, team interaction and environment); 9.5 Manage Team (track performance, give feedback, resolve issues, manage team changes); 9.6 Control Resources (ensure physical resources are available as planned, monitor planned vs actual use, take corrective action). Physical resources = equipment, materials, facilities, infrastructure; team resources = personnel (varied skills, full- or part-time, added or removed over time). Overlaps with Stakeholder Management; Section 9 covers the team subset of stakeholders. Key concepts: the team = individuals with assigned roles working toward a shared goal; invest effort in acquiring, managing, motivating and empowering it; involving all members in planning and decisions adds expertise and commitment; the PM is both leader and manager and responsible for forming an effective group, aware of team environment, geographic locations, communications, organisational change management, internal and external politics, cultural issues and organisational uniqueness; develops skills and competencies while keeping satisfaction and motivation; upholds professional and ethical behaviour. Physical resource management: allocate and use material, equipment and supplies efficiently; needs data on demand, configurations and supply; poor control is a risk (late critical equipment delays production; low-quality material causes recalls or rework; too much inventory raises costs, too little fails demand). Trends: shift from command and control to collaborative, supportive management empowering teams; optimise utilisation; resource management methods (lean, just-in-time manufacturing, Kaizen, total productive maintenance, theory of constraints) - adapt to what the organisation uses; emotional intelligence (inbound: self-management and self-awareness; outbound: relationship management; emotionally competent teams are more effective and have lower turnover); self-organising teams (agile, no centralised control; the PM - who may not be called that - provides environment and support and trusts the team; generalised specialists who adapt and accept feedback); virtual/distributed teams (enabled by email, audio and video conferencing, social media, web meetings; advantages - expertise from anywhere, home-based staff, people with mobility limitations or disabilities; challenges - isolation, knowledge-sharing gaps, tracking progress and productivity, time zones, culture). Tailoring: diversity, physical location, industry-specific resources, acquisition of team members (full/part-time), team development and special needs, life cycle approach. Agile: high-variability projects benefit from self-organising teams of generalising specialists; collaboration boosts productivity and innovative problem solving, integration, communication, knowledge sharing and flexible assignments.
